posts.quote: Every password I've ever made is my dog's name plus a number. The problem is I've had four dogs and I'm not good with numbers.
posts.caption: The bank locked me out at 7:40 on a Monday morning, which is a bold time to start anything. Three wrong guesses. I was so sure the first one was Biscuit, because Biscuit was the dog during the years I opened that account. Then I remembered it might have been during the Murphy years. Murphy had a number too. I think it was his birthday, but I never knew his birthday because we got him from a man in a Walmart parking lot. The reset email went to an address I stopped using in 2017. I am now on hold. The music is lovely.
posts.first: My husband keeps all of his passwords in a little notebook in the desk drawer labeled PASSWORDS in big block letters. I told him that's the first place a burglar would look. He said a burglar is welcome to his Netflix. I've started borrowing the notebook myself.

posts.quote: Please don't ask me for my honest opinion and then look at me like I keyed your car.
posts.caption: My friend Deb came out of the fitting room on Saturday in a lime green dress with ruffles at the shoulders and asked me to be completely honest. She said completely. She said it twice. So I told her it made her look like a very confident salad. I said it kindly. I even smiled. She stood there for a good ten seconds with the face of a woman whose car I had just walked past with a key. Then she bought the dress. She wore it to lunch the next day and sent me a photo. It still looked like a salad.
posts.first: I have been asked for my honest opinion maybe four hundred times in my life and it has gone well exactly twice. Both times it was about a casserole. I'm starting to think people want a mirror that talks, not a friend. I'm not available for that position.

posts.quote: It took me fifty years to find my personal style. Turns out it's anything without a button.
posts.caption: I cleaned out my closet on Sunday with the full intention of donating the things I no longer wear. Two hours in, the donate pile was almost everything I own, and the keep pile was three wrap dresses, a cardigan, and the pants with the stretchy waist. Every single thing in the donate pile had a button somewhere. Jeans, blazers, that blouse I bought for a wedding in 2011. I tried one of the blazers on for old times' sake. It fought me. I let it win, folded it, and drove the whole pile to the church bin before I could change my mind.
posts.first: My mother wore a girdle to the grocery store every week of her life and told me a lady always suffers a little. I think about her every time I tie a wrap dress. I love her. I just think the suffering could have stayed home.

posts.quote: My love language is you leaving the dishwasher the way I loaded it.
posts.caption: There is a system. Plates face the center, bowls go top rack at an angle, and nothing, not one fork, goes in handle down. I have explained this system to my husband an estimated three hundred times since 1999. Last night at 9:15 I opened the dishwasher to start it and found a cereal bowl wedged sideways across four plates like it was trying to escape. He was very proud of himself for helping. I said thank you. I meant it, mostly. Then I waited until he went upstairs and fixed it. Twenty-seven years. Still fixing it. Still saying thank you.
posts.first: My sister says I should just let it go and run it however he loads it. My sister also has a dishwasher that smells like a pond. I'm not taking advice from her on this one. I've accepted that I'll be reloading that thing until one of us dies.

posts.quote: My grandmother had a fur coat and a cocktail ring. I have a heated blanket and a coupon for 20 percent off. We are not the same.
posts.first: Grandma Ruth wore that cocktail ring to the Piggly Wiggly every Tuesday like she was attending a gala. I wore my heated blanket to the mailbox this morning. It has a cord. I had to unplug it first. She would have had a lot to say about that.

posts.quote: Anyone else get a text that says 'call me when you can' and immediately age three years?
posts.caption: My cousin Linda sent me five words on Thursday at 2:12 in the afternoon. Call me when you can. No emoji. No context. No period, which somehow made it worse. In the forty seconds before I called her back, I had mentally attended two funerals, sold the house, and drafted an apology for something I did at Thanksgiving in 2016. She picked up on the first ring. She wanted to know if I still had the recipe for the corn casserole. I gave it to her. Then I sat down in the big chair and stayed there for the rest of the day.
posts.first: I have asked my family to please put the reason in the text. Even one word. Casserole. Weather. Gossip. My son now sends call me when you can, nothing's wrong. I appreciate the effort. I still don't believe him for the first ten seconds.

posts.quote: The trees drop everything in October and everybody calls it beautiful. I drop one thing and it's 'are you okay?'
posts.caption: Tuesday afternoon outside the farmers market, the handle on my canvas bag gave up and eleven apples went rolling down the sidewalk in eleven directions. A man in a fleece vest stopped and asked if I was okay in the voice you use on someone standing on a ledge. A woman behind him asked if I needed to sit down. I did not need to sit down. I needed my apples. Meanwhile, the big maple across the street was dropping leaves by the thousand and people were stopping to take pictures of it. Nobody asked the maple if it was okay. Nobody ever does.
posts.first: I collected nine of the eleven apples. The other two rolled under a parked truck and I decided they belong to the truck now. I told my husband about it that night and he asked if I was okay. I made him sleep with the window open.

posts.quote: Kitchen Rules: If you didn't cook it, you don't get to season it.
posts.caption: I spent most of Sunday on a pot roast. Four hours, the good carrots, a splash of red in the pan because the recipe said so and I believe in following instructions. I set it on the table at 6. Before I had even sat down, my brother-in-law reached for the salt and shook it over his plate like he was putting out a fire. He hadn't tasted it. Not one bite. He just assumed. I watched him do it and said nothing, which my husband says was very mature of me. I've already decided what he's bringing to Thanksgiving. It's ice.
posts.first: My grandmother kept the salt shaker in her apron pocket during Sunday dinner for this exact reason. If you wanted it, you had to ask her, and she would look at you for a long time before handing it over. Nobody ever asked twice. I'm thinking about getting an apron.

posts.quote: I bought a $6 candle called 'Serenity' and I've been waiting all week for it to kick in.
posts.first: The candle has been burning on the kitchen windowsill since Monday night. So far this week the dryer has broken, the dog ate a sock, and I've been on hold with the cable company twice. It smells wonderful, though. I've lowered my expectations to smelling wonderful.

posts.quote: My favorite room in the house is whichever one nobody else is in.
posts.caption: There are four rooms on the first floor of this house and by 7 on a weeknight all four of them have someone in them. The TV is going in one. Someone is on speakerphone in the kitchen. The dog has claimed the couch and is not negotiating. So I've started taking my glass and a book upstairs to the little window at the end of the hall, the one nobody uses because it doesn't have an outlet. No outlet means no chargers, which means no visitors. I sat up there for an hour on Tuesday. Nobody noticed I was gone. Perfect.
posts.first: My husband found me up there last night and asked what I was doing. I said reading. He asked what I was reading. I held up the book. He stood there a little longer, so I turned the page very slowly and he finally went back downstairs. It's a good book.

posts.quote: I said I'd be there in five minutes. I meant that as a mood, not a measurement.
posts.caption: My friend Carol texted at 6:05 on Friday asking if I was still coming to trivia night. I wrote back on my way, five minutes. At that exact moment I was on the couch, barefoot, with half a glass of red and a show I'd been meaning to finish since August. I want to be clear that I believed it when I typed it. I did eventually go. I arrived at 6:50, right as they announced the round on state capitals, which I would not have helped with. Carol looked at her watch. I looked at the snacks. We both moved on.
posts.first: My husband has learned to translate. Five minutes means twenty. Ten minutes means I haven't found my shoes. On my way means I have thought about leaving. He just nods and starts the car around the twenty-minute mark. It's the most romantic thing he does.

posts.quote: I said yes to brunch three weeks ago because it felt so far away. Now it's tomorrow and I'd like to speak to whoever agreed to this.
posts.caption: Three weeks ago a woman from book club asked if I wanted to do brunch on a Sunday at the end of the month. In my mind the end of the month was so far away it practically didn't exist. Future me would be rested. Future me would have clean hair. So I said yes, sounds lovely, and went home. Tonight I opened the calendar and there it is, tomorrow at 10:30, circled in red in my own handwriting. Future me is here. She has none of those things. She is on the couch drafting a strongly worded note to her past self.
posts.first: I've started a new rule where I only agree to plans that fall within forty-eight hours. Anything further out and I'm signing a contract on behalf of a woman I've never met. My book club now says I'm hard to schedule. That's the idea, sweetheart.
